title: Structured outputs and tool calling
summary: Structured outputs make a model return data that matches a schema; tool calling lets it request actions your code runs. This lesson is the site's reference for both: the tool definition and its schema on Claude, OpenAI, Gemini and MCP, the round trip with its failure branches, four ways to get structured data with dated provider limits, and the agent-computer interface rules for tools a model can use, with one refund tool worked through the loop.

blocks.text: In a September 2025 post, Anthropic reports what it did to its own tools. Claude Code limits a tool response to 25,000 tokens by default; in one Slack example the concise response used about a third of the tokens of the detailed one; when it launched the web search tool it found Claude appending 2025 to the query and fixed that in the tool description; and Claude Sonnet 3.5 reached state-of-the-art on SWE-bench Verified after precise refinements to tool descriptions.

As of 2026-10, Anthropic's tool search documentation puts a number on catalog cost: a multiserver setup of GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana and Splunk can consume about 55k tokens in definitions before Claude does any work, and tool search typically reduces this by over 85 percent.

OpenAI recommends always enabling strict mode and says every schema generated in its Playground has it on. Its own design advice is to offload what the code knows: define submit_refund() with no parameters and pass the order_id from application code.

Google documents a failure that comes from a design habit: a prompt that requires structured text such as XML immediately before a tool call can make the call fail with Malformed_Function_Call, and Google's preferred workaround is a dedicated update() function that carries the notes.

The MCP specification says there SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations, and that clients SHOULD show tool inputs to the user before calling the server, to avoid malicious or accidental data exfiltration.

worked_example.title: Worked example: a refund tool, two failed calls and one executed call

blocks.text: A support agent has one tool, issue_refund. The example follows one request through the loop of subtopic 2 and shows what each check catches and what no schema can. The table fixes every input; the tool and the limits are this lesson's own assumptions, not vendor figures.

Cap on failed calls per request
Claude Sonnet 5.5 with the default auto

blocks.title: One request, call by call
items: The schema lists 3 required properties and forbids any other key (additionalProperties false); reason is an enum.
The user asks for a refund of 1,250 cents on order A-1001 because the parcel arrived damaged.
The first call sends amount_cents as the string '12.50'. The application's check rejects it before any side effect, so 0 calls reach the payment system.
The application answers with a tool_result, is_error true: 'Invalid amount_cents: Input should be a valid integer; got '12.50'. Fix it and call again.' That is 1 failed call so far.
The second call sends the integer 1250. The shape is valid, but the amount is 250 cents above the refundable balance, which no schema knows.
The application answers with another error result that names the limit: the amount exceeds the refundable balance of 1000 for A-1001, send at most 1000. That is 2 failed calls so far.
The third call sends 1000. All checks pass and the payment call carries the key request-abc:A-1001, so a repeat of a refund on that order in this request records one refund, not two.
With strict: true on this tool, Claude's strict mode guarantees the input matches the schema, so the first failure could not occur and 1 round trip is saved; the second failure would remain.

Two checks no schema carries. A call with amount_cents -5 is a valid integer, and Claude's strict mode cannot reject it because numeric constraints such as minimum are unsupported, so the code checks it: 'amount_cents must be a positive number of cents. Fix it and call again.' That is a failed call too.
A tool_use that names delete_everything gets the error result 'Unknown tool 'delete_everything'; the only tool is issue_refund.' and no refund code runs for it: 1 more failed call.

Had the third call failed too, the cap of 3 failed calls would end the loop, with 3 model requests and 0 payment calls in the stub run, and the user would see a handled error, not a fourth model turn. A limit of 8 turns ends a loop of successful calls the same way.

blocks.text: Schemas do not replace validation. The schema fixes the shape; whether the amount is positive and within the balance, and whether the tool exists, is the application's check, and on Claude the strict subset cannot express a minimum or a maximum at all.

The loop below is the same logic in code. It checks the tool name, the shape and the meaning before any side effect, sends no tool_choice, puts every tool_result of a turn in one user message with nothing before them, and returns the response untouched when stop_reason is anything but tool_use, so a refusal or a cut-off reaches the caller instead of being parsed.

blocks.code:
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, StrictInt, ValidationError

MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"
MAX_FAILED = 3                   # this lesson's cap on failed calls per request
REFUNDABLE = {"A-1001": 1000}    # cents, read from the system of record


class RefundArgs(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")        # additionalProperties: false
    order_id: str
    amount_cents: StrictInt                          # "12.50" fails, 1250 passes
    reason: Literal["damaged", "late", "other"]


TOOLS = [{
    "name": "issue_refund",
    "description": (
        "Refund part or all of one order to the customer's original payment method. "
        "Use it only after the customer has asked for a refund; do not use it to look up an order. "
        "amount_cents is a positive integer number of cents, at most the order's refundable balance. "
        "Returns the refund id."
    ),
    "input_schema": RefundArgs.model_json_schema(),
}]


class ToolLoopError(Exception):
    pass


def execute(block, request_id, payments):
    """Return (content, is_error) for one tool_use block."""
    if block.name != "issue_refund":                 # the model can name a tool that does not exist
        return (f"Unknown tool {block.name!r}; the only tool is issue_refund.", True)
    try:
        args = RefundArgs.model_validate(block.input)
    except ValidationError as e:
        err = e.errors()[0]
        return (f"Invalid {err['loc'][0]}: {err['msg']}; got {err['input']!r}. "
                "Fix it and call again.", True)
    if args.amount_cents <= 0:                       # a minimum is not in Claude's strict subset
        return ("amount_cents must be a positive number of cents. Fix it and call again.", True)
    limit = REFUNDABLE.get(args.order_id, 0)
    if args.amount_cents > limit:                    # meaning, which no schema knows
        return (f"amount_cents {args.amount_cents} exceeds the refundable balance "
                f"of {limit} for {args.order_id}. Send at most {limit}.", True)
    key = f"{request_id}:{args.order_id}"            # one refund per order per request, one key
    try:
        refund_id = payments.refund(args.order_id, args.amount_cents,
                                    idempotency_key=key, timeout=10)
    except TimeoutError:
        return ("The payment system did not answer within 10 seconds; the outcome is unknown. "
                "Repeating the same call is safe.", True)
    return f"Refunded {args.amount_cents} cents on {args.order_id}; refund id {refund_id}.", False


def run(client, payments, request_id, user_text, max_turns=8):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_text}]
    failed = 0
    for _ in range(max_turns):
        resp = client.messages.create(          # no tool_choice: any and tool return a 400 on this model
            model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
        if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            return resp                         # end_turn, refusal or max_tokens: the caller reads stop_reason
        results = []
        for block in resp.content:
            if block.type != "tool_use":
                continue
            content, is_error = execute(block, request_id, payments)
            result = {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": content}
            if is_error:
                result["is_error"] = True
                failed += 1
            results.append(result)
        if failed >= MAX_FAILED:
            raise ToolLoopError(f"{failed} failed tool calls; telling the user")
        # the assistant content goes back unchanged; every result of the turn goes in one user
        # message, tool_result blocks only, with no text before them
        messages += [{"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content},
                     {"role": "user", "content": results}]
    raise ToolLoopError("turn limit reached")


# usage: run(anthropic.Anthropic(), payments, "request-abc", "Refund 1,250 cents on order A-1001, it arrived damaged.")
blocks.caption: The refund loop on the Claude Messages API, checked against the message rules of subtopic 2 and run locally against a stub client that scripts the calls above, including the -5 and delete_everything cases. The model ID is the one in the structured outputs page's supported-models list.

subtopics.title: A tool is a name, a description and a schema, on every platform

blocks.text: A tool is a function the application offers to a model. The model never runs it: on Claude, OpenAI and Gemini the model returns a structured call and the application executes it. Anthropic describes a tool as a contract between a deterministic system and a non-deterministic agent, which is why the definition, not the code behind it, is what the model reads. The model sees a name, a description and a JSON Schema for the arguments; Anthropic calls the description by far the most important factor.
The idea is the same everywhere; the key names are not. The table is the mapping to use when a tool is ported from one platform to another.

blocks.caption: One tool in four vocabularies, as of 2026-10: the Claude Messages API, the OpenAI Responses API, the Gemini Interactions API and the MCP revision 2026-07-28.
rows: letters, digits, underscore and hyphen, 1 to 128 characters
a descriptive name such as get_weather; no pattern stated
descriptive, no spaces or special characters
SHOULD be 1 to 128 characters: letters, digits, underscore, hyphen, dot
strict: true; set it, because Chat Completions defaults to non-strict and Responses falls back to non-strict when the schema cannot be made strict
none: the server MUST validate inputs
a tool_use block with id, name, input
a function call with a call_id
a function_call step with name, arguments
a tools/call request with name, arguments
a tool_result with tool_use_id, optional is_error
a function_call_output with call_id: a string, format up to you
content, isError, optional structuredContent; resultType complete, or input_required when the server asks for more input

blocks.text: In the MCP revision named in the caption, a tool is a name, an optional title, a description, an inputSchema, an optional outputSchema, annotations and optional icons. The inputSchema must be a JSON Schema object, and the page's own example declares the older draft-07 dialect explicitly.

Without a $schema field the dialect defaults to 2020-12. A schema published by an MCP server is therefore not guaranteed to fit the subset a strict mode accepts (subtopic 4), so test a server's schema against the provider before turning strict on; this is the lesson's advice, not a spec rule. MCP's structuredContent is server-produced result data and, the page says, is unrelated to the structured outputs of a model. The protocol itself is taught in the MCP lesson.

subtopics.title: The round trip: the model proposes, your code executes

blocks.text: The diagram follows one tool-using request from the user to the answer and shows the ways a turn goes wrong: the model asks for something that fails your check, the tool itself fails, the model stops for a reason other than a tool call or an answer, or the loop reaches its own cap.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant U as User
  participant A as App
  participant M as Model
  participant S as Your system
  U->>A: request
  A->>M: messages, tool definitions
  loop until a turn has no tool call
    M-->>A: stop_reason and content
    alt tool_use
      Note over A: check name and input
      alt unknown name or bad input
        A->>M: tool_result, is_error
      else name and input valid
        A->>S: call, timeout, idempotency key
        alt call succeeds
          S-->>A: result
          A->>M: tool_result, same id
        else error or timeout
          S-->>A: error
          A->>M: tool_result, is_error
        end
      end
    else end_turn
      A-->>U: answer
    else any other stop_reason
      A-->>U: handled error
    end
    opt failed calls or turns reach the cap
      A-->>U: handled error
    end
  end
blocks.legend: The tool_use stop reason, the tool_result block and is_error are Claude's s3; a failed or invalid call can go back as an error result s3. Refusal and max_tokens end a structured response without a matching shape s5. Claude's other stop reasons (stop_sequence, pause_turn, model_context_window_exceeded, and a tool_use block cut off at max_tokens, where the fix is a larger max_tokens) are taught in the LLM fundamentals lesson, subtopic streaming and stop reasons; pause_turn only occurs with server tools. The loop cap, the timeout and the idempotency key are this lesson's convention; retries and keys are taught in the timeouts, retries and idempotency lesson. Sources: s3, s5.

blocks.text: The model only proposes. A call arrives with an id, a name and an input; your code runs it and answers with a result that carries the same id. The application, not the model, decides whether to run the call, how long to wait and whether to try again. Treat the input as untrusted data: a call can pass the schema and still be wrong, and MCP's own security section says servers MUST validate all tool inputs.
Claude rejects a conversation whose messages break the format, so the format is part of the contract. These are the rules the cited pages state as of 2026-10.

blocks.caption: Message rules on Claude. OpenAI and Gemini link each result to its call by call_id, and each also requires the model's own earlier output to be sent back as received: reasoning items on OpenAI, thought and function_call steps on Gemini.
rows: The tool_result goes in the user message that immediately follows the assistant message holding the tool_use.
a 400 error: tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after
In that user message the tool_result blocks come first and any text after them.
text before a tool_result causes a 400 error
Return every result of one assistant turn together, in one user message.
a separate message for each result teaches Claude to avoid parallel calls
Answer every tool_use, even a call you chose not to run.
send a tool_result with is_error true and a brief reason
Never send a tool_result for the tool search tool's own call, an id that starts srvtoolu_.

subtopics.title: Four ways to get structured data, and which to pick

blocks.text: A model can be asked for structured data in four ways, which differ in what the provider guarantees, not in the JSON Schema you write. Prompted JSON asks in the prompt and relies on parsing. A forced tool makes the schema a tool's input and requires the call. Native structured outputs put the schema in a response-format parameter. Constrained decoding on tool inputs is the strict flag. Anthropic describes its structured outputs as constrained decoding over a compiled grammar; OpenAI says its strict function mode is built on its Structured Outputs feature.

blocks.caption: Which mechanism to pick, as of 2026-10. Validate values in every row: a valid shape is not a correct answer [s11].

rows.pick_when: No schema-constrained mode exists for the model or platform, or the job is a prototype. Validate with a library and retry if needed, with a cap on attempts (this lesson's addition) [s9, s11].
rows.avoid_when: Downstream code cannot tolerate a missing key or a wrong type. OpenAI's JSON mode promises valid JSON, not your schema [s9].

rows.pick_when: The structured result is an action you will execute anyway, and the platform still supports forcing: OpenAI forces one function and Gemini's any mode requires a call [s8, s10].
rows.avoid_when: The newest Claude models reject it: any and tool return an error, and a forced call skips thinking (table in subtopic 7) [s2].
rows.example: Route a request to one handler function on OpenAI.

rows.pick_when: The answer itself must be a fixed JSON shape: extraction, classification, a report [s5, s9, s11].
rows.avoid_when: The schema needs keywords outside the provider's subset, or on Claude you use citations or prefilling, which conflict with it [s5].
rows.example: Extract name and plan interest from an email with output_config.format.

rows.pick_when: The model calls your functions and a wrong type or a missing key would break them: strict: true on Claude and on OpenAI (set it explicitly) [s5, s8].
rows.avoid_when: You use programmatic tool calling, which does not accept strict tools, or exceed Claude's per-request strict-tool limits [s5, s7]. Strict checks shape, not meaning.
rows.example: A booking function that needs the passenger count as an integer.

blocks.text: The common advice to force a single tool to get structured output is now a workaround on Claude: Anthropic names JSON outputs and strict tool use as its two structured-output features, and for models that reject forced tool use points to auto with strict tools or to structured outputs. The two also combine in one request, one shaping the answer and the other the calls.

Pick by where the structure sits. In the answer: native structured outputs. In a call the model makes: a strict tool. Neither offered for your model: prompt, validate and retry. This is the lesson's rule of thumb, not a vendor rule.

subtopics.title: Native structured outputs: what is guaranteed and what still goes wrong

blocks.text: On Claude, native structured outputs and strict tools compile the schema into a grammar, which is why an unsupported keyword fails up front instead of producing a bad answer later. The flow shows one request on Claude and the four ways it can end; only the normal end guarantees the shape.

steps.caption: The schema travels in the request, in output_config.format or on a strict tool.
The first use of a schema compiles it into a grammar and stores it.
A keyword outside the subset, or a schema too complex to compile, is a 400 error.
Later requests with the same schema reuse the stored grammar.
A normal end gives JSON that parses and matches the schema, apart from the capitalization of enum values.
A refusal is a normal response whose text may not match the schema.
A response cut off at max_tokens may be incomplete JSON.

blocks.legend: Edges are the stages one structured-output request passes through on Claude, not network calls. The grammar cache, the refusal and the complexity errors are Claude's s5; OpenAI documents the same refusal and cut-off cases s9. Sources: s5, s9.

blocks.text: Check stop_reason before you parse, and validate values after. A guaranteed shape still allows a refusal, a cut-off, a wrong enum capitalization and a plausible wrong number. On Claude, mark every property required if key order matters, and ask for a short explanation field, not reasoning.

subtopics.title: The agent-computer interface: choosing and describing tools

blocks.text: The agent-computer interface is the surface a model acts through: tool names, descriptions, parameters and results. A common error Anthropic has observed is tools that merely wrap existing API endpoints, because an agent has limited context where a program has cheap, abundant memory. This lesson is the site's reference for these rules; the agent and MCP lessons link here.

blocks.caption: Rules for the tools a model sees, with the page that states each.
rows: Build few tools for whole tasks
search_contacts or message_contact, not list_contacts; schedule_event, not list_users plus list_events plus create_event; get_customer_context, not three getters
one tool with an action parameter instead of create_pr, review_pr and merge_pr
asana_search and jira_search, asana_projects_search; prefix or suffix matters, so measure it on your evaluation
Describe it as to a new hire
what it does, when to use it and when not, what each parameter means, what it does not return; at least 3 to 4 sentences
use enums and object structure; toggle_light(on, off) allows an invalid call
Do not make the model fill what you know
define submit_refund() with no parameters and pass the order_id from your code; merge functions always called in sequence
input_examples must match the schema, and cost about 20 to 50 tokens, or 100 to 200 when nested; OpenAI warns examples may hurt reasoning models
Ask for an explanation, not reasoning
a parameter that asks for step-by-step reasoning may draw a reasoning_extraction refusal

blocks.text: Building few task-shaped tools and consolidating operations pull the same way, but a merged tool with an action parameter puts a read and a write behind one name. This lesson's convention is to keep writes in their own tools so that approval can attach to the tool. Google adds a failure to avoid: if a prompt requires structured text just before a tool call, the call can fail with Malformed_Function_Call, and the preferred fix is to put those notes inside a dedicated function call.

blocks.caption: How many tools to expose at once, as of 2026-10.
rows: selection accuracy degrades past 30 to 50 tools; tool search is for 10 or more tools or over 10k tokens of definitions
fewer than 20 functions at the start of a turn, a soft suggestion; tool_search exists on gpt-5.4 and later
keep the active set to 10 to 20 tools at most

blocks.text: Pass the intern test, OpenAI's phrase: could a person do the task with only what you gave the model? If they would ask questions, put the answers in the description.

subtopics.title: Results, errors and side effects: what goes back to the model

blocks.text: A result is part of the interface because it enters the context window. Return only high-signal fields: Anthropic found that resolving cryptic UUIDs into meaningful names, or even a 0-indexed scheme, significantly improved retrieval precision by reducing hallucinations. An agent may still need identifiers for the next call, so offer a concise or detailed choice as a parameter, and cap what comes back with an instruction on how to ask for less.

blocks.caption: Result-shaping figures Anthropic reports for its own tools (published September 2025).
rows: The same response, concise (identifiers left out)
Claude Code's default cap on one tool response

blocks.text: Return failures as results, not exceptions. On Claude, set is_error to true and say what went wrong and what to try: Rate limit exceeded, retry after 60 seconds, not failed. Anthropic says Claude retries an invalid call two to three times with corrections before apologizing. MCP separates protocol errors, such as an unknown tool, from tool execution errors, such as bad input or a business rule, which go in the result with isError true so the model can correct itself.

Validate arguments yourself even when a strict mode is on: the guarantee covers shape, not meaning, so check that ids exist, amounts are within limits and the caller is allowed to do it. MCP says servers MUST validate inputs and rate limit calls, and clients SHOULD ask the user to confirm sensitive operations. Treat tool results as untrusted too, since they can carry injected instructions.

A loop can repeat a call, so give each mutating tool an idempotency key derived from the business operation; the key design is taught in the timeouts, retries and idempotency lesson. As this lesson's convention, keep reading and writing tools apart so only the writes need approval. Anthropic's evaluation advice is to run realistic multi-call tasks and record accuracy, runtime, number of calls, tokens and errors; it says many redundant calls might suggest rightsizing pagination or token limits, and many invalid-parameter errors might suggest clearer descriptions or better examples.

subtopics.title: Steering the loop: tool choice and parallel calls

blocks.text: The tool choice setting decides whether the model may answer without a tool, must call one, or must call a particular one. Parallel settings decide whether one turn may carry several calls. The names differ per platform and the restrictions differ per model, so check the model you use.

blocks.caption: Controls per platform, as of 2026-10.
rows: mode any with an allowed_tools list
Limit to a subset, keep the tool list
One call at most per turn
disable_parallel_tool_use: true inside the tool_choice object
parallel_tool_calls: false, zero or one call

blocks.caption: Where forced tool use is rejected on Claude, as of 2026-10: any and tool fail, while auto and none still work.
rows: auto or none; adaptive thinking does not block forcing, but a forced call skips thinking
Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1
auto with strict tool use, or structured outputs

blocks.text: Where forcing works, the API prefills the turn, so the model writes no explanation before the call. Claude calls several tools in one turn by default and does not prescribe an order: independent read-only calls are usually safe to run concurrently, calls with side effects, shared state or ordering might be better run one after another, and a skipped call still gets an error result. OpenAI says built-in tools cannot join a parallel batch of functions, and Gemini names parallel and compositional calling.

Do not send one user message per result. Anthropic names that formatting error as the most common reason parallel calls stop happening, because it teaches the model to avoid them. Send all results of a turn together. The off switch for parallel calls goes inside the tool_choice object, not at the top level of the request.

subtopics.title: Large catalogs: tool search and programmatic tool calling

blocks.text: Tool definitions are input tokens on every request, and a long list also makes selection worse (the table in subtopic 5 gives each vendor's count). OpenAI says callable function definitions count against the context limit and are billed as input tokens. Claude has two answers: load tools on demand with tool search, or let the model call them from code so that intermediate results never enter its context.

With tool search you send every definition and set defer_loading to true on the ones to hide. The model then finds the ones it needs by regex or BM25 search, and the matching definitions are loaded into the context. At least one tool must stay non-deferred.

blocks.caption: Tool search facts, as of 2026-10.
rows: Definitions of a typical five-server setup (GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana, Splunk)
over 85 percent, by loading 3 to 5 tools
5 by default; the model may set a limit from 1 to 10,000
keep the 3 to 5 most used tools non-deferred
a deferred tool cannot carry cache_control (a 400 error); put the breakpoint on a non-deferred tool

blocks.text: Programmatic tool calling lets Claude write code that calls your tools inside a code execution container, rather than one model round trip per call. Anthropic's example checks budgets for 20 employees: the traditional way needs 20 round trips and pulls thousands of line items into the context, while one script returns only the employees over budget.

blocks.caption: Programmatic tool calling, as of 2026-10: what it needs and what it does not allow.
rows: the code execution tool at version code_execution_20260120 or later; each tool lists that caller in allowed_callers
the code pauses and the API returns a tool_use block with a caller field; you return the result and the code continues
strict tools, forcing it with tool_choice, disable_parallel_tool_use, tools from an MCP connector
a pending call times out after about 4 minutes; the reply must hold only tool_result blocks
allowed_callers is guidance, not a security boundary

Rewritten to format v2 / shape v11 from vendor documentation fetched 2026-10-16 (originally imported from the gigai 0.1.11.10 shipped course ai-forward-deployed-engineer, Claude through GigAI 0.1.11.10): eight subtopics (tool definition across Claude, OpenAI, Gemini and MCP; the round trip with an exhaustive failure diagram; a decision block on four structured-output mechanisms; native structured outputs with dated per-platform limits and a flow of the four ends; the agent-computer interface rules at full depth; results, errors and side effects; tool choice and parallel calls; tool search and programmatic tool calling), twelve dated sources, a refund-tool worked example with its loop code, five cited in-practice blocks. This lesson is now the site's canonical home of tool design.

Accepted after the second read and the fix-round verification: provenance.reviewed_by and reviewed_on set; no content change.
